title: Hardware tuning profiles pack — overview
author: Noah Patel
body:
## Summary
The **hardware tuning profiles pack** is a **versioned, runtime-consumable set of performance defaults** for Redwood’s inference runtime. It selects the best-known configuration per **GPU SKU** and **workload shape**, with explicit guardrails for safety (tail latency, OOM/fragmentation risk) and a deterministic override model for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

This page is the entry point for:
- What the profile pack is (and isn’t)
- Who owns it and how changes ship
- Supported hardware SKUs (H100, B200, L40S) and compatibility philosophy
- How selection and overrides work across **Hosted / Dedicated / Private**

For the authoritative schema and selection rules, see: **Profile schema and selection rules**.

---

## Why we are doing this
As our fleet becomes more heterogeneous (SKU variants, driver/CUDA drift, MIG/no-MIG, PCIe vs SXM), “default runtime tuning” becomes ambiguous and difficult to reason about. The profile pack makes tuning:
- **Repeatable:** same inputs → same profile selection
- **Observable:** profile_id/profile_version surfaced in metrics, logs, and debug endpoints
- **Safe to roll out:** canary + SLO gates + rollback semantics
- **Documented:** “expected behavior” pages per SKU describe trade-offs and failure modes

---

## What a “profile” contains (high level)
A profile is a named configuration bundle covering runtime knobs that materially affect latency/cost/stability:
- **Kernel selection / variants** (e.g., attention kernel choice and fallback conditions)
- **Scheduler & batching heuristics** (workload buckets, queue limits, prefill/decode prioritization)
- **KV cache / memory tuning** (allocator behavior, compaction thresholds, headroom targets)
- **Admission control / concurrency caps** (per-SKU limits based on safe headroom)
- **Host/container recommendations** where applicable (e.g., CPU pinning / NUMA guidance), clearly labeled as:
  - **Required** (Redwood-controlled environments)
  - **Best-effort** (Private/on-prem variability)

Profiles intentionally avoid “bespoke per-customer tuning” as the default. Controlled overrides exist, but are guardrailed and auditable.

---

## Non-goals
- Rewriting kernels for every model family; this project packages *known good* runtime behavior and incrementally improves selection/fallback.
- Recommending a unique tuning file per customer workload; instead we provide **workload buckets** and safe override levers.
- Hiding performance trade-offs; each profile must ship with an “expected behavior” spec and a rollback plan.

---

## Supported SKUs and current status
The profile pack is organized around **SKU families** (plus compatibility gates for driver/CUDA and known hardware variants).

| SKU | Typical usage at Redwood | Support status | Notes |
|-----|---------------------------|----------------|------|
| **NVIDIA H100** (SXM/PCIe) | Hosted + Dedicated primary high-performance tier | **GA** (v1.0+) | Default-enabled in Hosted via canary gating; Dedicated is opt-in by default (see rollout policy). |
| **NVIDIA L40S** | Cost-optimized pools; bursty workloads; some Dedicated | **GA** (v1.0+) | More sensitive to OOM/fragmentation; defaults emphasize headroom and stable concurrency caps. |
| **NVIDIA B200** | Early fleet / bring-up | **Preview** (v0.x / v1.0 with explicit pin) | Hard compatibility gate; requires explicit profile pin until fleet baselines stabilize. |

Compatibility is not just SKU. Selection considers a “hardware fingerprint” (SKU + form factor + driver/CUDA capability + MIG policy when applicable). When in doubt, we select a conservative profile or refuse unsafe defaults (see B200 notes).

---

## Artifact and lifecycle
### Where the profile pack lives
- The pack is shipped alongside the runtime (starting **runtime-1.22**) as a **versioned artifact** loaded at startup.
- In Redwood-controlled environments, fleet defaults are managed by the control plane, but final selection is enforced by the runtime (to avoid drift and ensure deterministic behavior).

### Versioning model
- Profiles are versioned (semantic-ish): **MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH**
  - MAJOR: schema changes or meaningfully different behavior requiring coordinated rollout
  - MINOR: new SKUs / improved defaults with stable schema
  - PATCH: safety fixes (e.g., headroom adjustments) intended for backport when warranted
- A runtime build reports:
  - **profile_pack_version**
  - **active_profile_id**
  - **hardware fingerprint** used for selection

### Ownership
Primary owners (engineering):
- **Runtime architecture / overall pack:** Noah Patel
- **Kernel variants & fallback rules:** Hiro Tanaka
- **Scheduling/batching policy:** Sofia Ivanova
- **KV cache / memory guardrails:** Omar El-Sayed, Samir Qureshi
- **Bench methodology / acceptance thresholds:** Claire Dubois, Rina Kobayashi
- **Rollout safety & SLO gating:** Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes
- **Dashboards/metrics:** Allison Grant

Change control expectations:
- Any change to defaults must include:
  1) benchmark-lab results for the required matrix subset
  2) perf-canary comparison (where applicable)
  3) updated expected-behavior notes if trade-offs change
  4) a rollback plan (kill switch / version pin)

---

## How profile selection works (conceptual)
Selection is **deterministic** and happens in two steps:

1) **Compatibility gate**
   - Validate the runtime has enough information to safely select (SKU, driver/CUDA, form factor, etc.).
   - If the environment is unsupported for the requested/default profile, behavior depends on deployment mode:
     - Hosted: fall back to a safe supported profile when possible; otherwise remove node/pool from serving.
     - Dedicated/Private: fail closed for unsafe combos unless operator explicitly overrides with an acknowledgement flag.

2) **Best-match selection**
   - Choose the most specific matching profile based on:
     - GPU SKU family (H100/L40S/B200)
     - Known sub-variants (e.g., PCIe vs SXM)
     - Model family constraints (e.g., long-context heavy decode)
     - Workload bucket (prompt/response length distribution; concurrency class)

The exact precedence and matching rules are defined in **Profile schema and selection rules**.

---

## Overrides and precedence by deployment mode
The pack supports controlled overrides, but we treat “override” as an operational decision with explicit guardrails.

### Common terms
- **Fleet default:** Redwood-chosen default profile for a pool/SKU.
- **Customer pin:** Customer/operator explicitly selects profile_version/profile_id (Dedicated/Private).
- **Runtime safety clamp:** Runtime-enforced bounds that prevent unsafe settings even if requested.

### Precedence order (high level)
1. **Runtime safety clamps (always win)**
   - Example: refuse concurrency above safe limit when memory headroom is insufficient.
2. **Explicit customer/operator pin (Dedicated/Private)**
3. **Control-plane / fleet defaults (Hosted; optionally Dedicated)**
4. **Runtime fallback default**

### Hosted
- Default behavior is driven by Redwood fleet policy.
- Overrides are limited to Redwood operators; changes roll out via canary cohorts.
- Rollback is accomplished via:
  - kill switch to disable pack usage
  - reverting fleet default profile_version

### Dedicated
- Default: **opt-in** for profile default changes (product/SRE policy) unless contract/SLO explicitly allows automatic upgrades.
- Customers can request:
  - profile_version pin (recommended)
  - profile_id pin (rare; only when we have a clear expected-behavior spec)
- All pins must be auditable and reversible.

### Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Operator chooses whether to accept Redwood defaults or pin versions.
- The runtime enforces compatibility checks and emits warnings when:
  - driver/CUDA is out of the supported range
  - the selected profile is “preview”
- Private installations may not support host-level knobs; those are treated as best-effort and called out in the per-SKU docs.

---

## Observability: what you should see when this is working
The pack is only useful if operators can quickly answer “what profile am I on and why?”. The runtime must surface:
- **active_profile_id** and **profile_pack_version** in:
  - startup logs
  - /health and debug endpoints
  - tracing span tags (where enabled)
- Metrics labeled by sku/profile_id (bounded cardinality):
  - end-to-end latency histograms
  - scheduler queueing time (e.g., scheduler_queue_ms)
  - kernel choice / fallback counters
  - KV cache metrics (hit rate where applicable, compaction time, fragmentation estimate)
  - OOM / allocation failure signals

Dashboards and alert thresholds are defined in: **Runtime profile observability dashboard spec**.

---

## Safety and rollback principles
- **Fail closed on unsafe combinations** (especially for B200 early fleet and unknown driver/CUDA combos).
- **Reversibility is required:** profile changes must be reversible within one release train and via on-call-accessible procedures.
- **Tail latency is the primary rollout gate:** we will not ship “better average throughput” at the expense of p99 regressions on mixed workloads.

SLO gates and canary policy are specified in: **Profile rollout SLO guardrails**.

---

## Quick FAQ
**Q: Is this a control-plane feature or a runtime feature?**
A: Selection enforcement lives in the runtime for determinism and safety. The control plane provides defaults, rollout cohorts, and visibility, but the runtime is the final authority on “what is safe to run.”

**Q: Can customers tune individual knobs instead of choosing a profile?**
A: In Private and some Dedicated cases, we allow restricted overrides, but the recommended mechanism is **profile_version pinning**. Individual knob overrides increase drift risk and are subject to safety clamps.

**Q: How do we handle driver/CUDA drift across regions?**
A: Profiles include explicit compatibility ranges. If drift occurs, the runtime either selects a compatible profile variant or refuses to serve if no safe mapping exists (depending on deployment mode and policy).

**Q: What is “Preview” support for B200?**
A: The runtime will detect B200 and enforce an explicit pin until fleet baselines stabilize. We track B200 readiness via a smaller smoke benchmark suite and elevated observability requirements.
